articles.title: 'Will Currency Notes Be Privatised?': Akhilesh Targets Centre Over RBI Tender For Banknote Material
articles.description:
Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav has accused the BJP-led Centre of attempting to privatise a sensitive aspect of India's currency note production after sharing a tender-related notice issued by an RBI-owned note printing company.

The former Uttar Pradesh chief minister questioned the government's intentions over a notice that allegedly invites expressions of interest from firms for the manufacture and supply of specialised polymer substrate sheets with security features for Indian banknotes.

'Will Even Currency Notes Be Privatised?'

In a post on X on Friday, Yadav criticised the move, asking whether the government was planning to privatise currency note production.

"Will even currency notes be privatised under the corrupt BJP regime now?" he wrote.

"The people of this country never imagined that the model of commission-taking would sink to such a level. If the country's currency itself is not self-reliant, how can the economy and the nation become self-reliant? Will the government itself also be outsourced now?" he added.

भ्रष्ट भाजपा राज में अब नोटों का भी प्राइवेटाइजेशन हो जाएगा क्या? कमीशनख़ोरी का मॉडल इस हद तक गिर जाएगा, देश की जनता ने सोचा न था। जब देश की मुद्रा ही आत्मनिर्भर नहीं होगी तो अर्थव्यवस्था और देश आत्मनिर्भर कैसे होगा? अब क्या सरकार भी आउटसोर्सिंग पर दे दी जाएगी?

इतने बड़े और... pic.twitter.com/rvyxRjY5rZ

— Akhilesh Yadav (@yadavakhilesh) July 17, 2026

Yadav Questions Tender Process

The SP chief also questioned the scope and intent of the tender, saying that the notice appears to be a formality rather than a serious attempt to invite bids.

"Behind issuing such a small, miserly tender for such a large and sensitive work, is there some hidden intention to merely complete a formality? It appears the arrangement has already been made and this exercise is only for show," he alleged.

He further claimed, "The BJP is not a government; it is a partner of profiteers."

ALSO READ: Sonam Wangchuk, On Hunger Strike For 20 Days, Taken To Hospital By Delhi Police

Tender Seeks Bids For Banknote Substrate

The notice shared by Yadav was purportedly issued by Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL), which is responsible for printing Indian currency notes.

According to the notice, the company has invited global expressions of interest from eligible bidders for the manufacture and supply of specialised polymer substrate sheets incorporating security features for Indian banknotes.

The tender states that bids will be opened on August 18.

articles.title: Tamil Nadu local body polls likely before April deadline: Minister Sengottaiyan
articles.description: Coimbatore, July 18 (IANS) Tamil Nadu Revenue Minister Sengottaiyan on Saturday said elections to local bodies would be conducted before the statutory deadline next April, while asserting that the State government would not permit irregularities in public works or municipal administration. Speaking to reporters at Coimbatore Airport, the Minister said the government was committed to ensuring transparency in governance and would take decisions only after proper scrutiny. His remarks came amid questions over delays in certain civic infrastructure projects and preparations for local body elections. Referring to the Race Course Road development project in Coimbatore, Sengottaiyan said the tender process had been put on hold following issues related to the sanction of additional funds. He stressed that the government would not allow any deviation from established procedures. “As long as Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay is heading the government, there should be no mistakes in the execution of public projects,” the Minister said, adding that every administrative decision was being taken with due diligence and in accordance with the law. On the conduct of elections to municipalities and other local self-government institutions, Sengottaiyan said the present term extends until next April and there was no immediate need to rush the process. “The deadline for holding elections to local bodies is next April. We have time until then and will proceed accordingly,” he said. The Minister also clarified that civic tenders could not be cancelled without valid reasons, noting that all government decisions were based on legal and administrative considerations rather than political expediency. Commenting on the transport sector, Sengottaiyan welcomed the decision of private omnibus operators to provide services under the fares fixed by the government. He said the earlier situation, in which operators allegedly had to incur unnecessary expenses to run their services, had changed. “They have now agreed to operate buses at the government-approved fare, and that is a positive development,” he said. On the issue of narcotics, the Minister said the Tamil Nadu and Kerala governments were working together to strengthen anti-drug enforcement and curb the trafficking of narcotic substances across state borders through coordinated action. --IANS aal/rad

articles.title: NIPU-2026: India’s New Urea Investment Policy Explained
articles.description: The Union Government’s approval of the National Investment Policy for Urea-2026 for Atmanirbhar Bharat, or NIPU-2026, marks an important attempt to revive large-scale investment in India’s domestic urea manufacturing industry. Approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the policy seeks to encourage the establishment of new gas-based urea manufacturing units and reduce the country’s continuing dependence on imports. The Fertiliser Association of India has welcomed the decision, describing it as a potentially transformative step towards closing the gap between rising urea demand and domestic production. However, the real significance of NIPU-2026 lies not merely in its promise of adding manufacturing capacity. The policy changes the way project costs, returns and foreign-exchange risks will be recognised under the fertiliser subsidy framework. For investors, these changes could improve project bankability. For the Government, they could bring greater cost transparency. For farmers, the policy is intended to provide a more dependable domestic supply of India’s most widely used nitrogenous fertiliser. For MSMEs, engineering firms, logistics providers and technology companies, the development of multiple new fertiliser plants could also create a substantial downstream industrial opportunity. What Has the Union Cabinet Approved? The Cabinet has approved NIPU-2026 as the successor to the New Investment Policy-2012, whose investment window expired in October 2019. The Government has identified three important changes under the new framework: Separation of fixed and variable costs for subsidy and cost-recognition purposes. Introduction of a defined Return on Equity range, with a floor of 12% and a ceiling of 16%. Conversion of the fixed cost component into Indian rupees after four years, based on the prevailing exchange rate, to reduce long-term foreign-exchange uncertainty. The Government estimates that these changes could generate savings of more than ₹250 crore for every plant established under NIPU-2026 compared with the earlier NIP-2012 framework. While the official Cabinet announcement confirms that new gas-based urea manufacturing units will be covered under the policy, it does not provide a detailed list of proposed locations, investors, commissioning schedules or plant-wise capacity. FAI and subsequent industry reports have indicated that the framework could facilitate the development of eight to nine new gas-based plants, collectively adding around 10 million metric tonnes of annual domestic capacity. This figure should, at this stage, be treated as an industry projection associated with the policy rather than a plant-wise commitment disclosed in the Cabinet’s official release. Why India Needs Another Urea Investment Policy India has expanded domestic urea production significantly during the past decade, but demand continues to rise. The Government’s July 2026 Cabinet note states that India currently has 33 operational urea manufacturing units with a total reassessed or installed capacity of 269.42 lakh metric tonnes, equivalent to approximately 26.94 million tonnes. The gap between domestic production and demand continues to be met through imports. Domestic urea production increased from approximately 225 lakh metric tonnes in 2014-15 to a record 314.07 lakh metric tonnes in 2023-24. Production stood at 306.67 lakh metric tonnes in 2024-25. The fact that actual production can exceed reassessed capacity reflects, among other factors, higher capacity utilisation and production beyond reassessed capacity under the New Urea Policy-2015. Despite these gains, imports remain necessary, especially during periods of strong seasonal demand. Between April and October 2025, India imported 58.62 lakh metric tonnes of agricultural-grade urea, compared with 24.76 lakh metric tonnes during the corresponding period of the previous year. The Government stated that the additional imports were required to meet higher Kharif demand and build stocks for the Rabi season. FAI estimates that India’s urea demand is increasing at close to 5% annually and could reach 40 million metric tonnes, while domestic output remains around 30 million tonnes. It estimates that imports account for approximately 26% of annual requirements. These figures underline the central policy challenge: India has expanded production, but consumption and agricultural demand are also growing. NIP-2012 Created Capacity, but Its Investment Window Closed NIPU-2026 is not India’s first attempt to attract fresh investment into urea manufacturing. The New Investment Policy-2012 was introduced to facilitate greenfield, brownfield, revival and expansion projects in the urea sector. Six new units were eventually established under the framework. Four of these units were developed through joint venture companies involving nominated public sector undertakings, while two were established by private companies. The investment window under NIP-2012 expired in October 2019. The six plants added approximately 76.2 lakh metric tonnes of annual capacity. Government data shows that this capacity expansion played a major role in increasing domestic urea production during the last decade. But after the expiration of the earlier policy, potential investors lacked a current framework defining how capital costs, returns, operational expenses and currency risks would be treated for new projects. NIPU-2026 is intended to fill that regulatory gap. Why Separating Fixed and Variable Costs Matters One of the most important structural changes under NIPU-2026 is the separation of fixed costs from variable costs. Fixed costs normally include expenses associated with plant construction, machinery, financing, depreciation and long-term infrastructure. Variable costs are linked more closely to production volumes and inputs, particularly natural gas, electricity, water, maintenance and other operational requirements. Under a regulated and subsidised industry, insufficient distinction between these categories can make project economics difficult to evaluate. Investors may struggle to estimate which costs will be recognised, how subsidy calculations will change when input prices fluctuate and whether efficiency improvements will be rewarded. By separating fixed and variable costs, NIPU-2026 could provide: Greater visibility over eligible capital expenditure. More transparent subsidy calculations. Better differentiation between plant investment and operating efficiency. Improved comparability among proposed projects. Stronger cost-monitoring mechanisms for the Government. This separation may also allow lenders to evaluate project cash flows more accurately because capital recovery and operational reimbursement can be assessed independently. The effectiveness of this reform will, however, depend on the detailed methodology used to determine eligible fixed costs, energy norms, gas consumption benchmarks and allowable variable expenses. The 12% to 16% RoE Band Is Designed to Improve Bankability Large fertiliser plants require substantial upfront capital and have long construction and operating cycles. Investors therefore require reasonable visibility over potential returns before committing funds. NIPU-2026 introduces a Return on Equity floor of 12% and a ceiling of 16%. The lower threshold gives investors a measure of return protection, while the upper limit protects the public subsidy system from providing unrestricted returns. From a project-finance perspective, the RoE band could make proposed plants more attractive to public sector companies, cooperatives and private investors. It may also help project sponsors secure debt financing by creating a clearer regulatory framework for expected equity returns. Nevertheless, RoE protection alone does not guarantee investment. Final decisions will also depend on: The recognised project cost. Debt financing rates. Gas availability and pricing. Land and infrastructure readiness. Environmental clearance timelines. Water availability. Pipeline connectivity. Payment and subsidy-settlement timelines. Technology selection. Construction and commissioning risk. The policy’s success will therefore depend on whether the final operational guidelines provide clarity on these issues. Foreign-Exchange Protection Addresses a Major Long-Term Risk Modern fertiliser plants often require imported technology, specialised equipment, engineering services and foreign-currency financing. Currency depreciation during the construction and early operational stages can significantly increase project costs. Under NIPU-2026, the fixed cost will be converted into Indian rupees after four years using the exchange rate prevailing at that point. This mechanism appears designed to balance two competing objectives. During the initial years, investors receive some protection against exchange-rate movements associated with imported equipment and project liabilities. After the four-year period, converting the fixed cost into rupees limits the Government’s indefinite exposure to currency fluctuations. This is especially relevant for plants with long operating lives. Without such a conversion mechanism, exchange-rate movements could continue influencing recognised fixed costs and subsidy calculations for an extended period. The four-year window should ideally correspond with the expected construction and stabilisation period. Detailed guidelines will need to clarify how delays, cost overruns, refinancing and staged commissioning will be treated. Understanding the Claimed ₹250 Crore Saving Per Plant The Cabinet announcement states that the changes under NIPU-2026 are expected to save more than ₹250 crore for each plant compared with NIP-2012. However, the initial Cabinet communication does not provide a detailed calculation explaining whether this represents: Lifetime subsidy savings. Lower foreign-exchange exposure. Reduced financing costs. More accurate capital-cost recognition. Savings arising from the RoE ceiling. Improved energy-efficiency assumptions. A combination of these factors. The estimate is nevertheless significant. If eight or nine plants are ultimately developed, a saving of more than ₹250 crore per unit could translate into aggregate lifecycle savings exceeding ₹2,000 crore, based on a simple multiplication of the Government’s per-plant estimate. This is an analytical projection and not a separate fiscal estimate announced by the Cabinet. The Government should consider publishing a detailed financial model or explanatory note so that investors and taxpayers can understand how the savings have been calculated. Import Substitution Will Improve Security, but Gas Dependence Remains NIPU-2026 is being positioned as an import-substitution policy. Increasing domestic production can reduce India’s exposure to international urea prices, shipping disruptions, export restrictions and geopolitical instability. Recent experience has shown that maintaining adequate supplies may require a rapid increase in imports during high-demand agricultural seasons. Producing more urea domestically can therefore provide several strategic benefits: Greater control over seasonal availability. Reduced exposure to overseas export restrictions. Lower dependence on international freight and port availability. Improved ability to build domestic buffer stocks. Greater supply certainty for farmers. Reduced vulnerability to sudden global urea price increases. However, gas-based domestic production does not completely eliminate external dependence. Natural gas is the principal feedstock for most Indian urea plants. The cost of urea subsidy consequently remains sensitive to fluctuations in natural gas prices, other raw-material costs and international urea prices. The Government has acknowledged that its expenditure on urea subsidy changes with gas and raw-material prices. India may therefore reduce its direct dependence on imported finished urea while continuing to face exposure to imported energy and LNG. For genuine long-term self-reliance, NIPU-2026 will need to be supported by a broader strategy covering domestic gas production, secure LNG contracts , pipeline infrastructure, energy-efficient technology, coal gasification where environmentally and economically viable, and the future use of low-carbon hydrogen. Two Additional Plants Are Already Part of the Capacity Pipeline NIPU-2026 will operate alongside urea projects that are already under execution. The Department of Fertilisers previously stated that plants at Namrup in Assam and Talcher in Odisha were under execution, with each having an annual capacity of 12.7 lakh metric tonnes. In June 2026, the Government said that two high-capacity units with a combined annual capacity of 25.4 lakh metric tonnes were expected to commence production. The addition of these projects and any subsequent NIPU-2026 plants could substantially improve domestic availability. However, the timing of commissioning will be critical because large fertiliser projects generally require several years for land acquisition, engineering, construction, gas connectivity, testing and commercial stabilisation. What NIPU-2026 Means for Farmers For farmers, the most important issue is not the financial structure of the policy but the timely availability and affordability of urea. The maximum retail price of urea has remained unchanged since 2018, with the Government absorbing variations in production and import costs through subsidy support. If NIPU-2026 successfully expands domestic capacity, it could: Improve availability during peak sowing seasons. Reduce the risk of regional shortages. Lower dependence on emergency imports. Strengthen buffer-stock management. Improve supply planning between the Centre and states. Reduce vulnerability to geopolitical disruptions. However, increasing production capacity should not be viewed as a substitute for balanced fertiliser use. India also needs to improve soil testing, nutrient-use efficiency, farmer awareness and the adoption of alternative products such as nano urea, organic fertilisers, bio-fertilisers and customised nutrient formulations. Uncontrolled growth in urea consumption can create soil imbalances and increase the Government’s subsidy exposure. Capacity expansion and responsible nutrient management must therefore proceed together. A Major Opportunity for Public, Private and Cooperative Investors The fertiliser sector already includes a mix of public sector enterprises, private companies and cooperative institutions. Government data for 2023-24 showed that private companies contributed the largest share of total fertiliser production, followed by cooperatives and public sector companies. NIPU-2026 could attract proposals from all three segments. Public sector and joint venture projects may benefit from access to state-supported infrastructure and institutional financing. Cooperative organisations can align production with farmer networks and distribution systems. Private investors may bring project-execution capabilities, technology partnerships and operational efficiencies. A competitive project-selection process will be essential. Proposed plants should be assessed on: Energy efficiency. Capital cost. Gas connectivity. Location relative to major agricultural markets. Water availability. Logistics infrastructure. Environmental performance. Construction readiness. Financial strength. Technology and safety standards. The Government must ensure that the policy does not encourage avoidable capacity in locations where feedstock, water or evacuation infrastructure is inadequate. NIPU-2026 Could Generate a Large MSME Supply-Chain Opportunity The development of eight or nine large fertiliser plants would have an impact far beyond the major project developers. Each plant would require a wide network of engineering, construction, equipment, technology and service providers. This could generate business opportunities for Indian MSMEs in areas including: Industrial fabrication and structural steel. Pipes, valves, flanges and fittings. Pumps and compressors. Boilers and heat-exchange systems. Electrical panels, cables and switchgear. Instrumentation and process-control equipment. Industrial automation and cybersecurity . Water and wastewater-treatment systems. Fire detection and safety equipment. Pollution-control and emissions-monitoring technology. Industrial gases and chemicals. Packaging and bag-handling systems. Warehousing and material handling. Rail, road and port logistics. Plant maintenance and shutdown services. Testing, inspection and certification. Workforce training and safety management. Digital twins, predictive maintenance and asset-monitoring platforms. For this opportunity to reach smaller enterprises, project developers should be encouraged to publish structured procurement plans, vendor-registration schedules and localisation targets. Large engineering, procurement and construction contractors should also be required to provide fair opportunities to qualified domestic MSMEs rather than concentrating orders among a limited set of established vendors. Timely payment provisions will be particularly important. MSMEs participating in capital-intensive industrial projects often face working-capital pressure when certification and payment cycles are delayed. Environmental Performance Must Be Built into Project Approvals Although NIPU-2026 is primarily an investment policy, new fertiliser plants will have significant environmental and resource implications. Urea manufacturing is energy intensive and requires natural gas, water, electricity and extensive process infrastructure. New projects must therefore be evaluated not only on capacity and financial returns but also on: Energy consumption per tonne. Carbon dioxide emissions. Water-use efficiency. Wastewater recycling. Ammonia leakage prevention. Process safety. Emissions monitoring. Heat recovery. Renewable electricity integration. Readiness for low-carbon hydrogen or alternative feedstocks. Plants commissioned under NIPU-2026 are likely to operate for several decades. Approving inefficient technology today could create long-term environmental and subsidy liabilities. India should therefore aim to establish plants that are globally competitive not only in scale but also in energy and emissions performance. Key Implementation Questions That Remain Unanswered The Cabinet approval establishes the broad policy direction, but several operational questions remain. The detailed notification will need to clarify: Eligibility Will NIPU-2026 cover only greenfield projects, or will brownfield expansion and revival projects also be eligible? Capacity and Location Will the Government prescribe standard plant capacities, preferred regions or proximity requirements for gas pipelines and agricultural markets? Gas Allocation Will eligible projects receive assured domestic gas, pooled gas or market-linked LNG? How will gas-supply interruptions be handled? Project-Cost Approval What methodology will be used to determine reasonable capital cost and prevent avoidable cost escalation? Return on Equity What factors will determine whether a project receives a return closer to 12% or 16%? Subsidy Settlement Will subsidy payments be subject to defined timelines and interest provisions in case of delay? Foreign-Exchange Conversion How will the four-year conversion rule apply if a plant faces construction delays or phased commissioning? Environmental Compliance Will projects have to meet enhanced energy, water and emissions benchmarks? Local Procurement Will the policy include domestic value-addition or MSME procurement obligations? Commissioning Deadlines Will project approvals lapse if financial closure, construction or commissioning milestones are not achieved? The answers to these questions will determine whether NIPU-2026 becomes an effective investment framework or remains primarily a statement of intent. FAI Calls Policy a Confidence-Building Measure Welcoming the decision, Dr Siba Prasad Mohanty, Co-Chairman of the Fertiliser Association of India, said: “NIPU-2026 tackles the major structural challenge in India’s fertiliser sector—the gap between rising demand and static local capacity. This policy offers investors the confidence they need and paves the way for India to become fully self-reliant in urea production.” FAI has also applauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Department of Fertilisers under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers for introducing the policy at a time when international supply disruptions have increased the importance of domestic fertiliser security. SMEStreet Analysis: A Necessary Policy, but Not a Standalone Solution NIPU-2026 addresses a genuine structural requirement. India needs additional urea capacity. The previous investment framework has expired. Import dependence remains material, and demand continues to rise. Investors require clarity on cost recognition, returns and currency exposure before committing capital to new plants. The separation of fixed and variable costs, introduction of a 12% to 16% RoE band and partial protection against foreign-exchange volatility are therefore meaningful reforms. However, the policy’s success cannot be measured by the number of proposals received. It should be measured by: Projects reaching financial closure. Plants being completed within approved costs and timelines. Reliable availability of gas. Lower import dependence. Improved energy efficiency. Transparent subsidy calculations. Timely subsidy settlements. Competitive procurement. Participation of domestic MSMEs. Reliable supplies to farmers. Measurable lifecycle savings for the Government. NIPU-2026 could become one of India’s most important agricultural-input manufacturing initiatives of the decade. But Cabinet approval is only the first stage. The next phase—detailed guidelines, project selection, financing, feedstock security and disciplined execution—will decide whether the policy genuinely delivers an Atmanirbhar urea ecosystem. Key Takeaways The Union Cabinet approved NIPU-2026 on July 15, 2026, to encourage investment in new gas-based urea plants. The policy separates fixed and variable costs for greater transparency. It provides a Return on Equity range of 12% to 16%. Fixed costs will be converted into Indian rupees after four years to limit foreign-exchange exposure. The Government estimates savings of more than ₹250 crore per plant compared with NIP-2012. FAI and industry reports expect the policy to facilitate eight to nine plants and around 10 million tonnes of additional capacity. Domestic production can reduce finished-urea imports, but gas availability and pricing will remain critical. The investment cycle could create significant opportunities for engineering, manufacturing, logistics and technology MSMEs. Detailed implementation guidelines will ultimately determine the policy’s financial and operational success. Disclaimer: This article is an independent policy analysis prepared by SMEStreet using the Union Cabinet announcement, Government of India data and statements attributed to the Fertiliser Association of India. Capacity projections relating to eight or nine new plants represent industry expectations available at the time of publication. Final project numbers, locations, investment commitments, eligibility conditions and implementation timelines will depend on detailed Government notifications and subsequent approvals.
